mcqs.q: Anemia is defined as:
opts: A haemoglobin level below the reference range for age and sex
mcqs.explain: Anemia is a decrease in haemoglobin below the reference level for the person's age and sex; it is a feature of disease, not a disease itself.

mcqs.q: The two basic mechanisms of anemia are:
opts: Inadequate red-cell production or a shortened red-cell lifespan
Too many platelets or too few white cells
High iron stores or excess vitamin B12
mcqs.explain: Anemia results either from inadequate RBC production or from a shortened RBC lifespan (loss or destruction); normal RBC survival is ~120 days.

mcqs.q: Which deficiency causes a MICROCYTIC anemia?
mcqs.explain: Iron deficiency (with thalassemia and chronic disease) causes microcytic anemia; B12/folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia.

mcqs.q: Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) are a classic sign of:
mcqs.explain: Koilonychia (spoon nails), along with brittle nails and pallor, is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia.

mcqs.q: A common ORAL manifestation across the anemias is:
opts: Glossitis, angular stomatitis and a burning/sore mouth
mcqs.explain: Anemia commonly causes glossitis, angular stomatitis, oral ulceration and burning-mouth symptoms.

mcqs.q: On a blood film, 'pencil cells' suggest, and 'sickle cells' suggest:
mcqs.explain: Pencil cells point to iron deficiency, whereas sickle cells on film point to sickle cell anemia.

mcqs.q: Elective surgery under general anaesthesia should generally NOT be performed when the haemoglobin is below:
mcqs.explain: Elective GA is avoided when Hb is below 10 g/dL; the patient should be stabilised at least 24 hours preoperatively.

mcqs.q: The most common anemia worldwide is:
mcqs.explain: Iron deficiency anemia is the commonest, affecting more than 3.5 billion people.

mcqs.q: Which can INHIBIT dietary iron absorption?
opts: Phytates, oxalates and the tannin in tea
mcqs.explain: Phytates, oxalates and phosphates in plant foods, and tannin in tea, inhibit iron absorption.

mcqs.q: Blue discoloration of the sclera may be seen in:
mcqs.explain: In iron deficiency the thin, transparent scleral collagen lets the underlying uvea show through, giving a bluish sclera.

mcqs.q: Plummer–Vinson (Paterson–Brown–Kelly) syndrome combines iron deficiency with:
opts: Atrophic glossitis and dysphagia from oesophageal webs
mcqs.explain: Plummer–Vinson = IDA + atrophic glossitis/angular cheilitis + dysphagia from oesophageal webs, with a risk of post-cricoid carcinoma.

mcqs.q: First-line treatment of iron deficiency anemia is:
opts: Oral ferrous sulfate for ≥3 months, plus treating the cause
mcqs.explain: Treat the cause and give oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg TDS for 3 months or more; parenteral iron if oral is not tolerated.

mcqs.q: A recognised side effect of oral iron therapy is:
mcqs.explain: Oral iron commonly causes nausea, constipation and black stools; liquid iron can also stain and erode teeth.

mcqs.q: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by deficiency of:
mcqs.explain: B12 and folate are needed for DNA synthesis; their deficiency causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia.

mcqs.q: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the:
opts: Terminal ileum, bound to gastric intrinsic factor
mcqs.explain: B12 binds intrinsic factor (from gastric parietal cells) and is absorbed in the terminal ileum; large liver stores delay symptoms for 5–10 years.

mcqs.q: Which feature is specific to vitamin B12 (not folate) deficiency?
opts: Neurological signs such as subacute combined degeneration of the cord
mcqs.explain: Only B12 deficiency adds neurological features — subacute combined degeneration, paraesthesia, ataxia and difficulty walking.

mcqs.q: Which agent is contraindicated in a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency?
mcqs.explain: Nitrous oxide interferes with vitamin B12 metabolism and is (theoretically) contraindicated in B12 deficiency.

mcqs.q: Sickle cell anemia is caused by:
opts: Replacement of glutamic acid by valine in the β-globin chain (HbS)
mcqs.explain: An autosomal recessive substitution of valine for glutamic acid in the β-globin chain produces haemoglobin S, which sickles.

mcqs.q: A sickle cell crisis is typically precipitated by:
opts: Infection, dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis or cold
mcqs.explain: Vaso-occlusive and other crises are triggered by infection, dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis and cold.

mcqs.q: If a sickle cell patient develops a vaso-occlusive crisis during an extraction, the immediate management is:
mcqs.explain: Give oxygen and correct the triggers (hydration, warmth); avoid aspirin (acidosis) and ensure good oxygenation.

mcqs.q: The radiographic 'stepladder' trabecular pattern and 'hair-on-end' skull are seen in:
mcqs.explain: Sickle cell anemia shows a 'stepladder' trabecular pattern, bone infarcts and a 'hair-on-end' skull with a dense lamina dura.

mcqs.q: In sickle cell anemia, painful jaw infarcts are clinically important because they:
opts: Can be mistaken for toothache (and pulpal necrosis may occur without dental disease)
mcqs.explain: Bony infarcts in the jaws can mimic toothache or osteomyelitis, and pulpal symptoms/necrosis may occur even without dental disease.

mcqs.q: Which local anaesthetic is best AVOIDED in sickle cell anemia?
mcqs.explain: Prilocaine is avoided because in overdose it can cause methaemoglobinaemia; aspirin is also avoided (acidosis can precipitate a crisis).

mcqs.q: Before surgery, antibiotic prophylaxis is advised in sickle cell patients mainly because:
opts: Splenic infarction leaves many functionally asplenic and immunocompromised
They are allergic to all anaesthetics
mcqs.explain: Repeated splenic infarction (autosplenectomy) impairs immunity, so prophylactic antimicrobials (penicillin V/clindamycin) are given for surgery and infections treated vigorously.

mcqs.q: The 'chipmunk' facies with spaced upper anterior teeth is characteristic of:
mcqs.explain: Marrow expansion in β-thalassemia enlarges the maxilla, giving a 'chipmunk' facies with spaced/migrated anterior teeth and malocclusion.

mcqs.q: Why may general anaesthesia be technically difficult in thalassemia?
opts: Maxillary enlargement can make intubation difficult
mcqs.explain: Enlargement of the maxilla in thalassemia can complicate intubation; GA is also avoided in severe anemia/cardiomyopathy from iron overload.

mcqs.q: Aplastic anemia is characterised by:
opts: Pancytopenia with a hypoplastic bone marrow
A microcytic film with low ferritin
mcqs.explain: Aplastic anemia is peripheral pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) with a hypoplastic/non-functioning marrow.

mcqs.q: Oral findings in aplastic anemia commonly include:
opts: Petechiae, pallor, ulceration and gingival bleeding
mcqs.explain: Thrombocytopenia and neutropenia produce petechiae, mucosal bleeding, ulceration, pallor and gingivitis/periodontitis.

mcqs.q: When is it best to perform necessary dental treatment in a patient with aplastic anemia?
opts: On the day of a platelet transfusion, after consulting the haematologist
mcqs.explain: Treatment is best done on the day of platelet transfusion with haematology consultation; sedation/GA are avoided and care is postponed until the WBC normalises.

mcqs.q: Which investigation screens for haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell and thalassemia?
mcqs.explain: Haemoglobin electrophoresis identifies abnormal haemoglobins (HbS, raised HbF, absent HbA), screening for haemoglobinopathies.

saqs.q: Define anemia and give the morphological (MCV) classification with examples.
saqs.a: Hb below the reference range for age/sex. Microcytic (<78): iron deficiency, thalassemia. Normocytic (80–98): haemolytic, blood loss, marrow failure. Macrocytic (>99): megaloblastic (B12/folate), liver/alcohol.

saqs.q: List the oral and cutaneous signs of anemia.
saqs.a: Cutaneous: pallor, brittle nails, koilonychia (iron deficiency). Oral: glossitis, angular stomatitis, sore mouth/ulceration, burning-mouth symptoms.

saqs.q: Outline the causes and dental relevance of iron deficiency anemia.
saqs.a: Causes: blood loss (GI/menstrual), low intake, poor absorption (phytates/tannin), raised needs. Dental: Plummer–Vinson (glossitis, dysphagia, post-cricoid cancer risk), candidiasis, aphthae; treat with oral ferrous sulfate ≥3 months.

saqs.q: Why is nitrous oxide contraindicated in megaloblastic (B12) anemia?
saqs.a: Nitrous oxide interferes with vitamin B12 metabolism, which can worsen the deficiency and its neurological effects (subacute combined degeneration).

saqs.q: Describe sickle cell anemia: cause, crises and oral/radiographic features.
saqs.a: Autosomal recessive HbS (valine for glutamic acid). Crises (vaso-occlusive/haemolytic/aplastic/sequestration) triggered by infection, dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis, cold. Oral: pallor, delayed eruption, jaw infarcts mimic toothache; X-ray: stepladder trabeculae, hair-on-end skull.

saqs.q: State the key dental precautions in sickle cell anemia.
saqs.a: Prefer LA; avoid prilocaine (methaemoglobinaemia) and aspirin (acidosis → crisis); avoid acidosis/hypotension; sedation only with ≥30% O₂; raise Hb ≥10 before GA; give antibiotic prophylaxis (asplenic).

saqs.q: Describe aplastic anemia and its dental management.
saqs.a: Pancytopenia with hypoplastic marrow → anemia, bleeding, infection. Dental: treat on a platelet-transfusion day with haematology input, LA OK, avoid sedation/GA, use antifibrinolytics, and postpone until the WBC normalises.
